children: 0514 GMT - HSBC maintains its neutral month-ahead conviction for U.S. Treasurys, U.S. rates strategist Dhiraj Narula says in a note. HSBC finds the current selloff to be increasingly stretched, he says. "But with renewed geopolitical risks and a very much 'live' September FOMC meeting, yield levels could remain choppy in the coming weeks," he says. (emese.bartha@wsj.com)

0511 GMT - Bitcoin edges lower in the Asia, pausing after crossing $82,000 but firmly above $80,000. The closely watched level was crossed overnight after comments from Fed Gov. Waller pared expectations of aggressive rate hikes. Analysts are looking for a sustained run above $80,000 to confirm an upturn after volatility followed August's surge. The gains in Ethereum, Ripple and other coins are encouraging, signaling that buying is spreading across the ecosystem, says Antonio Di Giacomo at XS.com. The upswing is also significant because of the challenging backdrop for risk assets. Bond yields remain elevated and markets continue to weigh the possibility of further rate hikes globally. Higher yields normally reduce the appeal of crypto, but it's withstanding the pressure in recent sessions, he says. Bitcoin last trades at $81,016 after touching $82,163. (fabiana.negrinochoa@wsj.com)

0511 GMT - HSBC raises its forecasts for U.S. Treasury yields across the curve, reflecting its view of a more hawkish distribution of potential pathways for monetary policy and a higher structural floor under long-dated Treasury yields, U.S. rates strategist Dhiraj Narula says in a note. HSBC's new two-year Treasury yield forecast is 4.20% for end-2026 versus 3.85% previously, and 3.95% for end-2027 versus 3.50% previously. It now sees the 10-year Treasury yield at 4.65% by end-2026, up from 4.30% previously, and rising to 4.75% by end-2027, having previously expected it at 4.40% by end of next year. The two-year Treasury yield trades 0.5 basis point higher at 4.338%, while the 10-year yield is up 0.2 basis point at 4.763%, according to Tradeweb. (emese.bartha@wsj.com)

0507 GMT - Developments in the Iran conflict alongside key macro data, most prominently U.S. CPI data on Sept. 11, will remain the key near-term catalysts for bond markets, SEB's Jussi Hiljanen says in a note. "We believe the policy-rate paths currently discounted in U.S and euro-area markets have become stretched on the upside; however, a durable decline in yields is likely to require clearer prospects of a sustainable resolution to the conflict," the chief rates strategist says. This would need to translate into lower energy prices and easing inflation pressures, allowing policy-rate expectations to turn less hawkish and bond yields to decline, he says. As for data, the most immediate key one is U.S. payrolls data for August on Friday. (emese.bartha@wsj.com)

0505 GMT - German 10-year Bund yields require a pronounced improvement in the Middle East, which could allow energy prices to decline, to return to SEB's target range below the current levels, chief rates strategist Jussi Hiljanen says in a note. "For the 10-year Bund to revert to our previous 3.10-3.30% target range, some positive news on the Iran conflict would likely be required," he says. Fading hopes of an Iran deal, the implications for European energy markets and the relatively resilient economy have contributed to higher bond yields across the curve, he says. The 10-year Bund yield closed at 3.35% on Thursday, according to LSEG. (emese.bartha@wsj.com)

0435 GMT - Thailand's consumer prices likely rose 2.31% on year in August, according to the median estimate of five economists polled by The Wall Street Journal. That would be sharper than July's 1.95% increase. Prices likely rose mainly due to higher domestic fuel prices last month, which could have pushed up transportation inflation, ANZ Research's Kausani Basak says in a report. However, inflationary pressures remain manageable and within the Bank of Thailand's 1%-3% target range, she adds. Given weaker growth momentum in 2Q, ANZ expects the BOT to hold its policy rate steady at 1.00% in October. Inflation data are due next week. (amanda.lee@wsj.com)

0411 GMT - Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas is likely to deliver one additional 25 bps rate hike in 4Q, despite August headline inflation easing, ING's Deepali Bhargava says in a note. Headline CPI cooled marginally to 6.1% on year in August from July's 6.2%. However, core CPI remained sticky at above 4% last month, while higher oil prices could keep headline inflation elevated. Rising food price risks from El Nino could also keep inflation above BSP's 2%-4% target range. These factors should keep the BSP focused on ensuring that inflation returns to target on a sustained basis, she says. The BSP has hiked rates thrice in a row this year. (amanda.lee@wsj.com)

0407 GMT - Japanese companies' repatriation of funds is unlikely to be a driver of yen strength in the near term, Citi strategists say in a note. However, if Japanese companies develop a more bearish view on the dollar-yen pair, they could repatriate assets or put in place forex hedges on their overseas assets, the U.S. bank says. Earnings reinvested abroad by Japanese companies make up a growing portion of their outstanding overseas investment, Citi says. The dollar is 0.4% higher at 156.41 yen following a 1.8% decline on Thursday. (kosaku.narioka@wsj.com; @kosakunarioka)

0338 GMT - South Korean memory-chip makers are likely to post softer-than-expected 3Q earnings due to the won's strength, Nomura analysts say. The won has strengthened against the dollar since its June peak, weighing on Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, both of which generate all their revenue in dollars, say the analysts led by CW Chung in a note. A 10% appreciation of the won could reduce the chip makers' profits by 12%, they note. FactSet data show the dollar weakened about 11% against the won over the past three months. Nomura expects Samsung and SK Hynix to post below-consensus operating profits of 107 trillion won and 77 trillion won, respectively, in 3Q. However, Nomura expects the negative foreign-exchange impact to be offset by higher chip prices amid tight supply. (kwanwoo.jun@wsj.com)

0333 GMT - The dollar will likely trade between 4.03 ringgit and 4.06 ringgit next week, with investors likely to remain cautious ahead of U.S. inflation data, Kenanga economists say in a note. An in-line CPI reading would open a retest of 4.030, while evidence of broadening services inflation could push the dollar toward 4.060 ringgit, they reckon. The Fed is expected to stand pat in September, with the first rate cut in 2Q, while Warsh's speech could be a test rather than policy signal, they say. Markets will also monitor U.S.-Iran developments and oil prices, with the ECB's expected 25bp hike likely to have limited spillover on the ringgit, they add. Kenanga expects the dollar to face resistance at 4.049 ringgit, with support at 4.030 ringgit. The dollar is flat at 4.0441 ringgit. (yingxian.wong@wsj.com)

0312 GMT - Indonesia will remain predominantly a consumer and adopter of foreign-built AI rather than a producer of frontier capabilities, keeping the government's "global AI player" ambition aspirational, BMI says in a note. The country remains dependent on hyperscaler infrastructure, imported chips and foreign foundation models. AI adoption is expected to rise, supported by favorable demographics, hyperscaler investment and policy momentum. However, persistent digital-talent shortages, uneven connectivity and the widening gap in AI adoption between developed and emerging economies are likely to constrain adoption, BMI says. Power constraints, including a coal-heavy generation mix and grid bottlenecks, could further limit AI infrastructure expansion, it adds. Formalizing the country's national AI road map and ethics regulations remains a key swing factor for governance and investment credibility, BMI says. (yingxian.wong@wsj.com)

0253 GMT - The Singapore dollar is steady against its U.S. counterpart in the Asian session, supported by reduced Fed rate-hike expectations. "Fed Governor Waller signaled support for holding rates this month if disinflation continues, prompting markets to pare" expectations for a Fed rate increase in September, analysts at CIMB's treasury and markets research say in a report. Regional currencies have rallied broadly on the dollar's weakness, the analysts add. The U.S. dollar is little changed at 1.2666 Singapore dollars, LSEG data show. (ronnie.harui@wsj.com)
